## Function

SIGLEC-5 is a sialic-acid-binding receptor expressed mainly on myeloid cells. Its cytoplasmic inhibitory motifs recruit phosphatases that dampen activation when the receptor engages appropriate sialylated ligands. It operates in a complicated locus alongside activating SIGLEC-14, whose similar extracellular region can complicate interpretation.

::: {.gene-mechanism}
::: {.gene-state}
**Inhibitory signal intact**

Myeloid activation is tuned rather than simply switched on.
:::
::: {.gene-flow-arrow}
→
:::
::: {.gene-state .gene-state-off}
**SIGLEC5 reduced**

Inhibitory tone may fall, but phenotype depends on ligands, cell type, and SIGLEC14 genotype/expression.
:::

## Relevance here

Hypomethylation in inflamed UC tissue could reflect altered regulation **or more SIGLEC5-expressing myeloid cells**. Bulk methylation cannot distinguish these explanations. Expression, cell deconvolution, and locus-aware genotyping are important.

## The paired-receptor complication

SIGLEC-5 carries inhibitory ITIM motifs, whereas the closely related SIGLEC-14 signals through DAP12. Human genetic variation can produce a SIGLEC14-null fusion genotype, changing the balance between receptors with similar ligand-binding domains. Functional work with group B *Streptococcus* showed that this paired system can alter neutrophil inflammatory responses [@ali2014siglecs].

## Consequence for a UC biomarker

An assay that does not resolve cell type and the SIGLEC5/SIGLEC14 locus can misattribute both methylation and expression. The most informative design combines genotype-aware mapping, neutrophil/monocyte abundance, receptor-specific protein reagents, ligand sialylation, and downstream phosphatase or DAP12 signaling.

<details><summary><strong>Why “less methylation = more inhibition” is too simple</strong></summary>

The CpG may not control the promoter, RNA may not track it, receptor occupancy matters, and the paired activating Siglec changes the biological balance.
</details>
